text: Seventeen years is long enough for a marriage to turn into a correspondence, and for a daughter to grow up in it as a photograph. Walter has been in the United States alone all that time; when his wife and their teenage girl finally arrive from Angola, the three of them fit into a one-bedroom apartment and discover how little room there is for the versions of each other they had been maintaining at a distance. Ekwa Msangi keeps the film to 101 minutes and mostly to those rooms, where the arguments are practical — who sleeps where, what is cooked, what money is for — and the real negotiation happens underneath them. Dance is the one thing the three have in common, and the film treats it less as a cure than as a language none of them needs to translate. The reunion is where the difficulty starts.

God keeps an apartment in Brussels, and He is a bad husband, a worse father, and a coward at the desk where He arranges other people's misfortunes. Jaco Van Dormael plays the premise straight: the machinery of creation is a home computer in a room nobody else may enter, and the family around it has the sullen air of people shut indoors on a wet Sunday. His daughter Ea is bored, which in that household counts as heresy. One of the film's European Film Awards went to its production designer, and the reason is in every shot of the flat: heaven assembled from yellowed wallpaper, laundry, and locked doors. What follows is a comedy of literal consequences, worked out over 114 minutes with the deadpan patience of someone who thinks blasphemy is mostly a matter of household detail.

The audience arrives already holding the ending: the two friends at the centre are on their way to becoming each other's enemy. Matthew Vaughn builds the film out of that foreknowledge rather than around it. Charles Xavier and Erik Lensherr meet before either has a title, a school, or a cause, at the stage where a strange ability is still a private embarrassment tested in empty rooms; the recruitment stretch that follows amounts to a series of job interviews with frightened teenagers. What keeps 132 minutes of superhero apparatus moving is the argument between the two men, which cannot be settled because one of them has reasons the other can only sympathise with. It is a large and expensive entertainment organised around a disagreement rather than a fight.

The morning after Christmas, a family on holiday in Thailand hears a noise from the sea that none of them can place in time. J. A. Bayona spends the film on physical facts: what moving water does to a body, how far debris travels, how long a person can hold on to a tree. The wave is staged as an event happening to muscle and lung rather than to a landscape, and what comes after it is a matter of distances — a hospital corridor, a wrecked road, the impossibility of knowing where the others have ended up. Maria and Henry brought three sons on this trip, and the film never lets that number out of sight. At 113 minutes it is a disaster picture built almost entirely at eye level, which is what makes it hard to sit through.

Debt did it: Yeon-hee's family came apart over money, and the world she is left standing in has no sympathy to spare. Yang Ji-eun's film does not explain that world; it shows a young woman moving through it with the wariness of someone who has learned what people will do for a sum. Then there is Seo-jin, unruly and unafraid in a way Yeon-hee is not, and the friendship works like an open window in a shut room. The film describes its own subject in animal terms, a grazing creature discovering an appetite, and across 100 minutes it takes that literally enough to be uncomfortable. What it watches most closely is the point where a habit of enduring turns into a habit of wanting, and how short the distance between them turns out to be.

The premise is a distinction without much of a difference: hard cases cross paths with worse ones, and the city keeps score. Frank Miller films pulp at full strength — men who narrate themselves in the past tense, women introduced by what they want from someone, rooms lit as though light were rationed. None of it is offered as psychology. The stories cross rather than combine, so a face that dominates twenty minutes can disappear into somebody else's night, and the 102 minutes are divided among them without much concern for balance. What the film is after is a texture: crime fiction reduced to silhouette and narration, delivered flat, with the moral scale compressed until the only thing left to establish is which kind of bad a given character is.

Victor is sixty-something and out of patience with the present, including his marriage, so he pays a company to rebuild the week, forty years back, in which he met his wife. The comedy comes from the machinery. Someone has to direct this reconstruction, call the cues, keep an actress in character while the client falls for her exactly as he is paying to, and decide how much accuracy a customer can stand. Nicolas Bedos keeps two marriages in view at once, the remembered one and the worn one still going on at home, and lets neither settle into the flattering version. Across 115 minutes what stays unsettled is what exactly is being bought: a woman, a week, or the man Victor was before he had disappointed anyone.

An actress walks off a set in the middle of a working day and spends the rest of the film as nobody's character. What Touko finds instead is three strangers' worth of conversation: a man named Nagano in her passenger seat whom she has never met, Kikuchi, a screenwriter who used to write, at a small theatre, and Yasuko at the zoo. Kayo Nakamura gives each meeting the room to go nowhere. Eighty-three minutes is brief for a film in three movements, and the brevity is the discipline — nothing accumulates into a plot, nobody is repaired, the encounters stop when the day does. The interest lies in how differently a person talks to someone she will not meet again, and in the odd ease of a professional performer with no one around to watch her.

Half the platoon is gone before the film has settled, and the survivors are handed to a captain who enjoys the work. What follows moves downward: from the fighting inside the ruins, where a street is measured in cellars and a day's gain is one floor of one building, to the cruelty behind the line, where a captain's temper carries the force of an order. Joseph Vilsmaier gives 134 minutes to the parts a war picture usually skips — cold, bread, boots, the waiting, the wounded. When the lieutenant decides to take his men out of the city, it reads as arithmetic rather than defiance. The Soviet army stays largely off screen, encircling and unseen, because by that stage the men in frame have found other things to be afraid of.
